# Complete diagonal parameterization of tetrahedral quadrilateral sections

This note parameterizes every proper quadrilateral section of a tetrahedron
and gives its centroid, cap fraction, and scalar centroid correction data
as rational functions. It also disproves uniqueness of a section with a
given centroid and a given 2-versus-2 vertex partition. It does not classify
all inverse images of the centroid map or prove the weighted-section bound.

Let T have vertices v_0,...,v_3 and barycentric coordinates ξ_0,...,ξ_3.
Fix the partition {0,1}|{2,3}. All relative volumes below are divided by |T|.

## 1. Bijection with an interior diagonal-intersection point

Every plane that strictly separates v_0,v_1 from v_2,v_3 cuts T in a convex
quadrilateral. Its four vertices, in cyclic order, lie on edges 02,03,13,12.
Its diagonals meet in a unique point e in the interior of T. Conversely,
for every e with positive barycentric coordinates

    (x,y,z,w),                 x+y+z+w=1,

the unique plane whose raw affine values at the four vertices are

    t=(1/x,1/y,-1/z,-1/w)                              (1)

has a quadrilateral section with diagonal intersection e. Multiplying all
four values by the same nonzero scalar only changes normalization or
orientation of the same plane.

Proof: the four edge intersections have coordinates

    A=(x,0,z,0)/(x+z),     B=(x,0,0,w)/(x+w),
    C=(0,y,0,w)/(y+w),     D=(0,y,z,0)/(y+z).

The two diagonal representations are

    e=(x+z)A+(y+w)C=(x+w)B+(y+z)D.

Thus these four points are coplanar and have e in both diagonals. Conversely,
if a diagonal intersection e is given, its representations on the two
pairs of disjoint tetrahedral edges determine exactly these four endpoints.
They determine the plane, which is (1). This proves the bijection without
any assumption that the positive or negative vertex values are distinct.

## 2. Exact centroid map

The centroid of any planar convex quadrilateral with cyclic vertices
A,B,C,D and diagonal intersection e is

    g_Q=(A+B+C+D-e)/3.                                 (2)

To prove this, triangulate along AC. If τ is the area fraction of triangle
ABC, then e=(1-τ)B+τD, because the areas are proportional to the respective
heights over AC. The area-weighted triangle centroids give
3g_Q=A+C+τB+(1-τ)D=A+B+C+D-e.

Consequently the barycentric coordinates λ of the section centroid are

    3λ_0=x[1/(x+z)+1/(x+w)-1],
    3λ_1=y[1/(y+z)+1/(y+w)-1],
    3λ_2=z[1/(x+z)+1/(y+z)-1],
    3λ_3=w[1/(x+w)+1/(y+w)-1].                         (3)

They are positive, sum to one, and satisfy sum_i t_i λ_i=0. Positivity and
the plane equation also follow geometrically from the centroid being in
the relative interior of the quadrilateral.

## 3. Cap fraction and coarea vector

Put

    P=x+y,       R=z+w=1-P,       a=xy,       b=zw,
    D=(x+z)(x+w)(y+z)(y+w)
      =(a-b)^2+aR+bP >0.                               (4)

For the cap on the {0,1} side of (1), its volume fraction is

    F=b(P-a+b)/D.                                      (5)

The complementary fraction is a(R+a-b)/D; the two numerators sum to D.
If u_raw=gradient(sum_i t_i ξ_i), its coarea section factor is

    [area(Q)/|u_raw|]/|T|=3xyzw/D.                      (6)

In particular the effective section-normal vector, divided by |T|, is

    (3xyzw/D)[gradient ξ_0/x+gradient ξ_1/y
                         -gradient ξ_2/z-gradient ξ_3/w].           (7)

Here and below area denotes Euclidean two-dimensional section area.

One direct derivation, which also covers repeated values, uses the section
triangulation ABC,ACD. For a general raw value vector (p,q,-r,-s), the
normalized coarea factors of those two triangles are 3α and 3δ, with

    α=ps/[(p+r)(p+s)(q+s)],
    δ=qr/[(p+r)(q+s)(q+r)].

For example cone(v_0,ABC) has volume fraction pα by taking the determinant
of the three edge differences; dividing this cone volume by its height
p/|u_raw| gives its section coarea. The ACD determinant gives δ identically.
The cap is triangulated by the two cones from v_0 over ABC,ACD, together
with tetrahedron(v_0,v_1,C,D). The latter has relative volume
q^2/[(q+r)(q+s)]. Thus

    F=p(α+δ)+q^2/[(q+r)(q+s)].

Substitute p=1/x,q=1/y,r=1/z,s=1/w. Then

    α=xyzw/[(x+z)(x+w)(y+w)],
    δ=xyzw/[(x+z)(y+w)(y+z)],
    α+δ=xyzw/D.

The cap formula simplifies to (5), and (6) follows at once. All denominators
in this computation are strictly positive; no divided difference or generic
value assumption is used.

Let g_T be the ordinary tetrahedral centroid, and translate the common
section centroid g_Q to 0. The scalar quantity relevant to a possible
centroid correction is

    s_Q=area(Q)[u_unit·(g_T-g_Q)]/|T|.

Since the affine value of g_Q in (1) is zero and that of g_T is
(1/x+1/y-1/z-1/w)/4, equations (4) and (6) give the especially simple formula

    s_Q=3[bP-aR]/(4D).                                (8)

Both F and s_Q are rational functions of the diagonal point e, and (3)
is the exact compatibility condition for sharing a section centroid with
any other plane.

## 4. The centroid map is not one-to-one, even within one partition

Choose 0<z<1/8 and positive x,y satisfying

    x+y=1-2z,               xy=z+z^2.

Equivalently

    x,y=[1-2z ± sqrt(1-8z)]/2.

For e=(x,y,z,z), formula (3) gives

    λ=(A,A,B,B),
    A=(1+z)/3,              B=(1-2z)/6.                 (9)

Indeed λ_0=λ_1 follows from
(x+z)(y+z)=2z, and λ_2=λ_3=(1-2z)/6. Swapping x and y gives a second,
distinct plane with the same centroid. A third plane has diagonal point
(A,A,B,B); its section centroid equals that same point, by (3), because
A+B=1/2. It separates the same vertex partition. Thus a presumed unique
quad section for each centroid and each partition would omit real sections.

A rational example is

    e_1=(12,7,3,3)/25,       e_2=(7,12,3,3)/25,
    λ=(56,56,19,19)/150.

The three different planes can be written with respective raw value vectors

    (7,12,-28,-28),
    (12,7,-28,-28),
    (19,19,-56,-56).

All are proper quadrilateral sections with centroid λ. Each of the first
two caps has volume fraction 4/25 and scalar moment -111/400. These small
individual cap fractions do not refute the weighted stationary-section
inequality: they have not been combined into a balanced circuit with a
mean below 27/64.

The parameterization (1)–(8) is general. The symmetric example in this last
section serves only to certify a failure of inverse uniqueness, not as a
substitute for analyzing arbitrary common centroids.

## 5. A global concave–convex shortcut also fails

A plane of the fixed partition through a prescribed interior λ can be
parameterized independently by (u,v) in (0,1)^2, with raw values

    (u/λ_0, (1-u)/λ_1, -v/λ_2, -(1-v)/λ_3).

The affine value at λ is zero. It is tempting to infer uniqueness of the
centroidal section from global concavity in u and convexity in v of the cap
fraction. The asserted convexity in v is false even when every λ_i<1/3.

Take

    λ=(8/25,31/100,1/20,8/25),     u=3/5,
    v_-=9/1000,  v_0=1/100,  v_+=11/1000.

The exact cap fractions, using the positive-denominator triangulation
formula in section 3, are respectively

    268399175000/502765515771,
    2347280500/4419318981,
    35793986575000/67735924512529.

Their centered second difference is

    F(v_-)+F(v_+)-2F(v_0)
      =-216696601290923321682823000
        /135221182702189782497027701155183 <0.

These planes are not claimed to have centroid λ; they only pass through it.
The certificate rules out the proposed global concave–convex optimization
shortcut, not a possible local saddle classification at actual stationary
sections.

## 6. Within-pair ordering in the central centroid region

The general centroid formulas imply the exact identities

    3(λ_0-λ_1)=(x-y)[b-(a-b)^2]/D,
    3(λ_2-λ_3)=(z-w)[a-(a-b)^2]/D.                     (10)

For example, after dividing the first difference by x-y, the two relevant
fractions combine as

    z/[(x+z)(y+z)]+w/[(x+w)(y+w)]-1
      =[R(a-b)+2b-D]/D=[b-(a-b)^2]/D.

The equality case x=y follows by continuity, or directly from (3).

If every λ_i<=1/3, both bracketed factors in (10) are strictly positive.
Indeed the inequalities λ_0,λ_1<=1/3 are respectively equivalent to

    ax<=b(1+x),          ay<=b(1+y).

With X=max(x,y)>=sqrt(a) and k=a-b, they imply kX<=b. If k^2>=b, then
k must be positive: for k<=0, |k|<=b<1 gives k^2<b. Thus k>=sqrt(b) and
a>b, so kX>=sqrt(ab)>b, a contradiction. This proves k^2<b. The other
pair proves k^2<a in the same way.

Consequently, in this central region λ_0-λ_1 has exactly the sign of x-y,
and λ_2-λ_3 has exactly the sign of z-w. This rules out the within-pair
fold responsible for the example in section 4 when all four centroid
coordinates are at most 1/3. It does not yet imply global injectivity of
the full three-dimensional centroid map.
